claims.title: Portuguese reach the uninhabited islands
claims.summary: Portuguese navigators, by tradition João de Santarém and Pero Escobar, reached São Tomé and Príncipe, finding the equatorial islands entirely uninhabited and suited to bases for mainland trade.

claims.title: São Tomé settled by Álvaro Caminha
claims.summary: The first successful settlement of São Tomé was established under a crown grant to Álvaro Caminha, beginning the islands' colonisation.

claims.title: Deportation of Jewish children and convicts
claims.summary: The early colonists included Portuguese degredados and some two thousand children taken from expelled Jewish families and deported to be raised as Christians, most of whom died — part of the forced human mixture that founded Creole society.

claims.summary: The smaller island of Príncipe was settled under a similar crown arrangement, extending Portuguese control over the archipelago.

claims.summary: Settlers planted sugar cane worked by enslaved Africans, creating one of the earliest Atlantic plantation economies — a model later exported to Brazil and the Caribbean.

claims.title: São Tomé a leading sugar producer
claims.summary: The number of sugar mills grew to around sixty, making São Tomé Africa's foremost sugar exporter and for a time one of the world's largest producers.

claims.title: The Angolar maroon community
claims.summary: Escaped slaves formed independent communities in the forested interior; the Angolares, of disputed origin, settled the rugged south and lived by fishing, rejecting plantation labour.

claims.title: The revolt of Rei Amador
claims.summary: Rei Amador united maroons and plantation slaves in a great revolt that overran much of São Tomé, one of the largest slave uprisings of the Atlantic world.

claims.title: Capture and execution of Rei Amador
claims.summary: After his forces had held much of the island, Amador was captured and executed by the Portuguese; he endured as a hero of resistance and is now honoured as a national figure.

claims.summary: Coffee and then cocoa, brought from Brazil around the 1820s, were planted on the islands, reviving the plantation economy after the long decline of sugar.

claims.summary: Portugal began abolishing slavery in its empire, with an 1869 decree and full emancipation completed in the 1870s — though forced contract labour soon took its place.

claims.summary: Worked by the roças and their contract labourers, São Tomé became for a time the world's leading producer of cocoa.

claims.title: Cadbury and the cocoa boycott
claims.summary: After Joseph Burtt's report confirmed the abuses, the chocolate firms Cadbury, Fry and Rowntree announced a boycott of São Tomé cocoa, an international scandal that shamed Portugal but left coerced labour largely intact.

claims.title: The Batepá massacre
claims.summary: Under Governor Carlos Gorgulho, colonial police and settlers killed many Forro islanders who resisted forced labour — a massacre, with the toll uncertain, that became the founding memory of São Toméan nationalism.
